```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines); pair with fig.height
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}

# keeps a prompt and its answer space on one PDF page: place `r nq(...)` on its
# own line just above the prompt. Emits nothing in non-LaTeX output. lines =
# lines of prompt text, rows = rows of blank space below it (0.3 in each),
# extra = any other height (in inches), e.g. a figure or table
nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}

bd <- read.csv("../data/BdPondSurvey.csv")
temp <- bd$water_temp_c
swabbed <- bd$frogs_swabbed
positive <- bd$bd_positive

# log posterior: binomial likelihood + Normal(0, 10) priors on a and b
log_post <- function(par, x = temp) {
  sum(dbinom(positive, swabbed, plogis(par[1] + par[2] * x), log = TRUE)) +
    sum(dnorm(par, 0, 10, log = TRUE))
}
check_diff <- log_post(c(1, -0.1)) - log_post(c(3, -0.2))
```

## The scenario

The pond in Act 1 was one of 12 ponds the field crew surveyed in the
same summer. At each pond they swabbed a sample of frogs and recorded
the water temperature. Bd grows poorly in warm water, so managers want
to know whether infection is less common in warmer ponds, and if so,
by how much. Here are the survey results (the Act 1 pond is P11):

```{r bd-data}
knitr::kable(bd, align = "cccc",
             col.names = c("Pond", "Water temp. (°C)", "Frogs swabbed", "Bd positive"))
```

```{r bd-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.6}
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(temp, positive / swabbed, pch = 16, ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1,
     xlab = "Water temperature (°C)", ylab = "Proportion Bd positive")
```

Use a logistic model: the number of positives at pond $i$ is binomial
with $n_i$ frogs swabbed and infection probability $p_i$, where
$$\log\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i} = a + b\,T_i$$
and $T_i$ is the water temperature. Give both $a$ and $b$ a
Normal(0, 10) prior (wide enough that any signal from the data will overpower it!).
You'll fit this model with your own Metropolis sampler.

**How much does the chance of infection change with temperature, and
how uncertain is that change?**

Try Part 1 on paper first, before you open a laptop or start typing
code.

`r nq(3, 8)`

## Part 2: Fit it (laptop, ~60 min)

**Using AI:** we recommend no AI for all of Part 2. Each task is short,
and writing and debugging this code yourself is the point of the lab.
R's help pages, web search, and classmates are fine. After each
question, circle how you actually used AI.

**What to turn in:** your filled-in answers and your 2c figure as an
image (upload in WebCampus). You don't need to submit your code.

The data are in `BdPondSurvey.csv` (columns `pond`, `water_temp_c`,
`frogs_swabbed`, `bd_positive`), on the course website:
<https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/BdPondSurvey.csv>.
You can read it straight from that link:

```{r data-url, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
data_url <- "https://kevintshoemaker.github.io/NRES-746/data/BdPondSurvey.csv"
bd <- read.csv(data_url)
```

Or paste the data into R directly:

```{r data-code, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
water_temp_c  <- c(10.0, 12.3, 14.9, 15.8, 17.6, 17.9, 18.6, 18.8, 19.0, 20.5, 21.7, 22.1)
frogs_swabbed <- c(21, 18, 23, 19, 18, 24, 16, 17, 23, 23, 20, 18)
bd_positive   <- c(13, 12, 8, 9, 6, 8, 3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 1)
```

```{r data-code-check}
# the pasted vectors above must match the CSV
stopifnot(all.equal(temp, c(10.0, 12.3, 14.9, 15.8, 17.6, 17.9, 18.6, 18.8, 19.0, 20.5, 21.7, 22.1)),
          all.equal(swabbed, c(21, 18, 23, 19, 18, 24, 16, 17, 23, 23, 20, 18)),
          all.equal(positive, c(13, 12, 8, 9, 6, 8, 3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 1)))
```

## Reflection (~10 min)

In Act 1, the Wald and credible intervals for one pond's prevalence
disagreed sharply. How closely did they agree for $b$ here, and why
might that be? What would you tell the managers about Bd and water
temperature, in a sentence or two they could act on?
